title: Zero to One, part 2: competition is for losers

linkedin.text:
"Competition is for losers." That's Peter Thiel, and it's the most misunderstood idea in Zero to One.

He doesn't mean don't work hard. He means: if your business is the same as ten others, all ten of you will cut prices until nobody makes real money.

Walk through any market where ten shops sell the same phones on the same street. The customers win. The owners fight over thin margins.

What I'd take from part two:

1. Aim for a business with no close substitute. That's what lets you keep your margins and plan for years, not weeks.

2. Be honest about your market. Copycats define it so narrowly they look unique. The real test: what else could your customer buy instead?

3. Build what's hard to copy: technology that's 10x better, network effects, economies of scale, and a brand people trust.

4. Start small and win it completely. Amazon started with books, Facebook with one university, PayPal with eBay's power sellers.

5. Don't pick fights with giants. Rivalry makes you copy them instead of building something new.

Part 2 of 4 on the business lessons in Zero to One. Next: why being last can beat being first.

Chat: Roland, isn't competition good for business? ⚔️ Good for customers, yes. For your profits? Thiel's answer is no.

Chat: Lesson 4: competition kills profit 📉 When ten businesses sell the same thing, they cut prices until nobody makes real money. A business with no close substitute keeps its margins and can plan for years, not weeks.

Chat: Lesson 5: be honest about your market 🎭 Copycats describe their market so narrowly they look unique: "the only Ghanaian restaurant in Lekki". Ask the real question: what else could your customer buy instead?

Chat: Lesson 6: what makes a business hard to copy 🏰 1. Technology that's 10x better, not 10% better 2. Network effects: it gets better as more people use it 3. Economies of scale: it gets cheaper as it grows 4. A brand people trust

Chat: Lesson 7: start small, then dominate 🎯 Amazon started with books. Facebook started at one university. PayPal started with eBay's power sellers. Win a small market completely, then expand step by step.
Chat: Lesson 8: don't chase "disruption" 💥 Picking a fight with giants makes you their target. And rivalry makes you copy your rival instead of building something new.
